intro:
The exercises in this chapter all push toward one habit: treating a secure service boundary as a set of explicit, reviewable decisions rather than a single library call. You decide where public TLS terminates, which proxy headers you believe, which peers must prove their identity, how certificates rotate without downtime, and which HTTP defaults keep browsers honest. Each exercise isolates one of those decisions so it can be argued about in review and asserted against in CI.

The through-line is that almost everything here is policy you encode in plain Rust types, not behavior you hope a framework supplies. A typed `ServiceEdge` or `HttpSecurityPolicy` makes the termination owner, the forwarded-proto trust rule, the cookie flags, and the rotation window visible in one place. That visibility is the whole point: a boundary you can read and test is a boundary you can keep secure as the deployment changes underneath it.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose a TLS termination strategy from the real deployment boundary
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The point of this exercise is to choose termination from the trust boundary in front of you, not from a default habit. Walk the four cases against three questions the chapter raised: who owns the public certificate, who trusts the proxy headers, and who needs the peer identity directly.

The browser-facing API behind a cloud load balancer naturally wants load-balancer termination. The load balancer already owns the public certificate (the cloud provider issues, renews, and serves it), so the Rust service never sees raw TLS for that hop. The consequence you must accept is that the service learns the original scheme only from a forwarded header, so forwarded-proto trust must be tied to the load balancer hop and stripped from anything arriving directly.

The internal admin tool on the same host as a reverse proxy fits reverse-proxy termination. The proxy and the app share a host, so the plaintext segment between them never leaves the machine, and the proxy can own the certificate and add the security headers in one place. This is the case where same-host reverse-proxy termination keeps the trust boundary smallest while still centralizing certificate handling.

The service-mesh deployment already has a sidecar trust boundary. TLS terminates in the sidecar, and the verified peer identity (the SPIFFE-style identity the mesh issues) is handed to the app out of band. You should model that identity handoff explicitly rather than assume "inside the mesh means trusted," because the whole value of the sidecar is that the peer identity becomes a policy input.

The dedicated edge appliance written in Rust most plausibly wants in-process TLS. It owns the full external edge, there is no upstream proxy to delegate to, and packaging the trust store and certificate lifecycle into the binary is the honest contract for an appliance. This is the case to justify with certificate ownership and packaging: the appliance ships and renews its own material, so it should terminate TLS itself. Across the four cases you have at least three distinct strategies, justified by trust-header policy (load balancer) and certificate ownership and packaging (the appliance), and none of them pretends one strategy fits every service.
criteria: Four cases produce three distinct strategies: load-balancer, same-host reverse-proxy, sidecar, and in-process.
Load-balancer choice is justified by forwarded-proto / trust-header policy; the appliance choice by certificate ownership and packaging.
The answer explicitly states that termination strategy depends on the boundary and that no single strategy is universally correct.

exerciseSolutions.title: Identify insecure HTTP, cookie, and header settings in one API edge
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Read each field as a policy statement and ask not "does the app still work" but "does the boundary stay safe under real browsers and proxies."

The settings that weaken transport or session safety directly are: `cookie.secure = false` lets the session cookie travel over plaintext HTTP, so any plaintext request leaks it; `cookie.http_only = false` exposes the cookie to JavaScript, turning any XSS into session theft; `redirect_http = false` leaves a plaintext entry point that a network attacker can sit on and downgrade; and `hsts_max_age_secs = 0` means the browser never pins HTTPS, so the first request and any later typed URL can be intercepted before the redirect. Those four are unsafe on their own.

The combination problem is `allowed_origin = "*"` together with credentialed requests. A wildcard CORS origin is relatively harmless for anonymous public data, but the moment the API serves credentialed responses (cookies, Authorization headers) it becomes a path for arbitrary origins to read authenticated responses. `same_site = "None"` compounds this: it tells the browser to send the session cookie on cross-site requests, which is exactly what you do not want for an authenticated session, and `SameSite=None` is only valid alongside `Secure`, which is off here, so the pairing is both dangerous and inconsistent.

Everything here that a local demo tolerated should differ in production. A demo over `http://localhost` has no plaintext-network adversary and no cross-origin browser, so `Secure=false`, no redirect, no HSTS, and wildcard CORS feel harmless. In production those same values are the boundary's weak points. The secure replacements are: `Secure=true` and `HttpOnly=true` on the cookie, `SameSite=Lax` (or `Strict` for an admin session), `redirect_http=true`, a non-zero HSTS max-age (one to two years), and a single exact origin instead of `*`.

In CI, assert the policy and not just reachability. Concretely: assert that the `Set-Cookie` header carries `Secure` and `HttpOnly` and a non-`None` `SameSite`; assert that a plaintext request receives a redirect to HTTPS; assert that a successful HTTPS response carries a `Strict-Transport-Security` header with a non-zero max-age; and assert that the CORS response echoes only the configured origin, never `*`, on credentialed routes.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: An audit predicate per field turns the insecure config into a list of CI-checkable boundary rules.
criteria: Names more than three concrete insecure settings: Secure=false, HttpOnly=false, redirect off, HSTS=0, and SameSite=None.
Proposes secure replacements for cookies (Secure/HttpOnly/Lax), redirects, exact-origin CORS, and non-zero HSTS, each with a stated risk.
Lists CI assertions for secure cookie flags, redirect-to-HTTPS behavior, HSTS presence, and exact-origin CORS.

exerciseSolutions.title: Harden one API edge configuration deliberately
exerciseSolutions.solution:
This is a boundary-policy exercise, not a framework exercise. The goal is to take the insecure defaults and express them as small typed Rust values whose secure shape is obvious to a reviewer and assertable by a test.

Keep the config as plain structs with one method per derived property, exactly as the chapter's `https_tls_security_defaults` example does. The hardening is four concrete moves. First, turn `redirect_http` on so there is no plaintext entry point. Second, harden the session cookie: `secure = true` so it never travels over plaintext, `http_only = true` so script cannot read it, and a `same_site` that is not `"None"` (`Lax` is the calm default for a browser session). Naming the cookie with the `__Host-` prefix is a small extra: that prefix is only honored when the cookie is `Secure`, has `Path=/`, and carries no `Domain`, so the name itself encodes part of the policy. Third, replace the wildcard origin with one exact origin so `cors_mode()` reports `locked-down`. Fourth, give HSTS a non-zero max-age so `hsts_enabled()` is true and reinforces the redirect.

The `is_hardened()` predicate captures why these belong together: a cookie is hardened only when `Secure && HttpOnly && same_site != "None"`. Encoding that as one method means the next CI step asserts a single boolean instead of re-deriving the rule. Likewise `hsts = redirect_http && hsts_max_age_secs > 0` insists that HSTS and the redirect reinforce each other; advertising HSTS while still serving plaintext would be contradictory, so the predicate ties them.

The summary then prints exactly the four lines the lab expects, each proving one value changed: `redirect = true`, `cookie hardened = true`, `cors = locked-down`, `hsts = true`. Because the values are explicit and typed, the diff in review is small and the assertions in CI are direct.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The hardened config: each field is an explicit policy statement a reviewer reads and a test asserts.
criteria: redirect_http is true and a non-zero HSTS max-age makes the hsts predicate true, so redirect and HSTS reinforce each other.
The cookie sets Secure and HttpOnly (plus a non-None SameSite), so is_hardened() returns true.
allowed_origin is one exact host, so cors_mode() reports locked-down rather than wildcard.
main prints the four expected lines, proving each value changed.

exerciseSolutions.title: Debug a TLS failure without weakening verification
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Most TLS failures are evidence problems before they are code problems, so the repair path is a checklist that gathers evidence first and never ends with "turn verification off."

Start from the four questions the chapter mapped to the four ways a handshake fails. (1) Hostname / SNI: does the certificate's subject-alternative-name set actually cover the host the client asked for, and is the client sending the right SNI through the proxy? A name mismatch is the single most common cause, so check it first. (2) Full chain: did the server send its leaf plus any intermediates, or is it serving only the leaf so the client cannot build a path to a trusted root? A freshly rotated certificate that omits a new intermediate fails exactly this way. (3) Trust store: does the client trust the root that signed the chain, or did rotation move to a CA the staging trust store does not carry? (4) ALPN: did both sides agree on a protocol (for example `h2` versus `http/1.1`), since a protocol mismatch can surface as a generic handshake failure.

Critically, the proxy is a prime suspect here precisely because two things changed at once: the certificate rotated and traffic moved to a different proxy layer. A proxy or termination change can look exactly like a certificate bug to the app. The proxy might present its own certificate for a hostname the client did not expect, might forward to a backend whose SNI no longer matches, or might terminate TLS and then forward over plaintext while sending a forwarded-proto header the app distrusts so the app believes the request was plaintext. So before blaming the leaf certificate, confirm which hop actually produced the error and whether the forwarded-scheme trust changed with the new proxy.

Reproduce with explicit trust material, never by skipping checks. Stand up a local CA you control, issue a leaf with the right SANs, and point the client at that trust bundle: this exercises the same chain assembly and hostname verification a real client performs, so a green local run is meaningful. In CI, run the same local-CA harness so the assertion lives in the pipeline. The one acceptable concession is scope: a global `--insecure` / skip-verify switch is fine for a single throwaway local probe to confirm the network route reaches the right box, but it is never an acceptable production workaround, because it removes exactly the guarantee TLS exists to provide. The production fix is to correct the chain, SANs, trust store, or proxy configuration, not to stop verifying.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The checklist ordered by likelihood, with the local-CA reproduction in place of any skip-verify switch.
criteria: The checklist starts from hostname/SNI, then chain, trust store, ALPN, and proxy evidence, in likelihood order.
Disabling verification is explicitly ruled out as a production fix; only a single throwaway local probe is conceded.
Reproduction uses a local CA and explicit trust bundle in CI, exercising real chain and hostname verification.
Names concrete ways a proxy or termination change masquerades as a certificate bug: wrong presented cert, SNI mismatch, distrusted forwarded-proto after plaintext forwarding.

exerciseSolutions.title: Design certificate rotation and mTLS boundaries for a service fleet
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Rotation and mTLS go wrong quietly, so the work here is to pin down four things up front: how certificates renew, how the running process reloads them, how trust material reaches every peer, and where a verified peer identity becomes an allow or deny decision. Settle those while the fleet is healthy, not during the first expiry or half-finished rollout.

Classify the hops by who needs to prove what. The public API needs server-authenticated TLS only: browsers and external callers verify the server, and the server does not generally hold a client certificate for each browser, so requiring client certs there would be wrong. The internal queue consumer talks to a broker; if the broker authenticates clients by certificate it is mTLS, but if the broker uses a token or network ACL and only the transport must be encrypted, server-auth TLS plus a separate credential is enough, so treat it as server-auth TLS unless the broker policy demands client certs. The service-to-service path that requires mTLS is the clear mTLS hop: both ends present certificates and each verifies the other. So at minimum the public API is server-auth-only and the service-to-service path is mTLS.

Decide where peer identity is enforced and own it deliberately. mTLS is worth nothing if the verified peer identity is not turned into a policy input somewhere explicit. In a mesh, the sidecar can verify the certificate, but the authorization decision ("is this peer allowed to call this route") should land in the service, because only the service knows which identities its routes permit. If you instead enforce at a reverse proxy, the proxy must forward the verified identity to the app in a header that the app trusts only from that proxy hop. The appropriate owner is the component that holds the route-to-identity policy; pushing the check there keeps the boundary reviewable.

Reload without downtime is the transition teams miss: renewing the material on disk and actually loading it into the running process are two separate events. With 30-day rotation and a zero-downtime requirement, renew well before expiry (a 14-day `renew_before_days` window, as in the chapter's `rotate_now` predicate), write the new material, and trigger a hot reload of the certificate resolver and trust bundle rather than a process restart. Distribute the new trust root before issuing leaves from it, so a peer that already trusts the new root accepts both old and new during the overlap. That overlap window is what makes a mixed rollout safe.

Watch the signals that warn before users do. At minimum track a certificate-expiry horizon (days remaining per certificate, alert before the renew window closes) and a reload-failure count (renewed on disk but the process never picked it up is the classic silent failure). Add an mTLS-rejection rate so a rollout that distributes a new root unevenly shows up as peers being rejected rather than as a vague latency spike. Those three together cover the failure modes that rotation introduces.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote:
Hops classified by peer-auth and identity owner, with rotation as a renew-before-horizon predicate. Expected output:
public-api: ServerAuthOnly, identity at n/a
queue-consumer: ServerAuthOnly, identity at broker-token
svc-to-svc: Mtls, identity at in-process route policy
rotate now at 12 days left = true
signals: cert-expiry-horizon, reload-failure-count, mtls-rejection-rate
criteria: Classifies the public API (and queue consumer) as server-auth-only and the service-to-service path as mTLS.
Locates peer-identity enforcement at the component holding route-to-identity policy and justifies that owner.
Gives a concrete rotation strategy: renew before a 14-day horizon, distribute new root first, hot-reload without restart.
Names at least two observability signals: cert-expiry horizon, reload-failure count, and mTLS-rejection rate.

exerciseSolutions.title: Test HTTPS locally and in CI with realistic trust behavior
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The whole point is to test the secure path itself, not a weakened stand-in, so the plan is built around a trusted local CA rather than any skip-verification bypass. CI should prove policy, not just reachability.

Local certificate coverage: issue leaves from a CA you control with SANs that match exactly the hostnames the tests use. For browser-facing tests cover the app host (for example `app.localhost` or `app.test`); for the service-to-service test cover the internal service name the client dials. Cover both the bare host and any aliases the harness uses, because a missing SAN is the most common reason a realistic local test fails. Wildcard SANs are acceptable only if production also uses them; otherwise mirror the production SAN shape so the chain and hostname check behave the same.

Trust material in CI: install the local CA root into the browser/client harness's trust store (or pass it as an explicit trust bundle to the test client), and have the servers present leaves issued by that CA. This is the safe substitute for `--insecure`: the client performs full chain assembly and hostname verification against material you provisioned, so a passing test means the real verification path works. Never set a global skip-verify flag in the harness, because then the tests stop testing the thing that matters.

Validate both mTLS directions explicitly. The acceptance test: a client presenting a valid leaf signed by the trusted client CA connects and is authorized. The rejection test, which is the one teams forget: a client presenting no certificate, or one signed by an untrusted CA, or one with the wrong identity, is rejected at the handshake or by the identity policy. Asserting the rejection path is what proves mTLS is actually enforced rather than merely offered.

The CI smoke test must assert transport policy beyond "the port opens over TLS." At least: a plaintext request returns a redirect to HTTPS; a successful HTTPS response carries `Strict-Transport-Security` with a non-zero max-age; the session `Set-Cookie` carries `Secure` and `HttpOnly` and a non-`None` `SameSite`; and a cross-origin request is answered with the one configured origin, never `*`, on credentialed routes. Because the same local CA and the same SAN shape are used in development and CI, the trust behavior the tests exercise stays close enough to production that a green pipeline is meaningful evidence and not a false comfort.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The CI plan as code: trusted local-CA root, matching SANs, mTLS accept/reject, and four transport-policy assertions.
criteria: Uses a local/CI CA root installed in the client trust store rather than a verification bypass.
Includes both an mTLS acceptance test and an mTLS rejection test (untrusted or missing client cert).
Asserts at least three transport-policy properties: HTTPS redirect, Secure cookie, HSTS, and exact-origin CORS.
Keeps local and CI trust behavior production-like by sharing the same local CA and SAN shape, so a green pipeline is meaningful.

labSolution.expectedOutput:
redirect = true
cookie hardened = true
cors = locked-down
hsts = true
labSolution.explanation:
The lab starts from the insecure defaults (redirect off, a cookie with Secure and HttpOnly false and SameSite "None", a wildcard CORS origin, and a zero HSTS max-age) and asks you to make four deliberate hardening moves so the four printed predicates flip to their secure values.

The cookie becomes hardened because is_hardened() returns secure && http_only && same_site != "None"; setting secure and http_only to true and SameSite to "Lax" satisfies all three terms, so the second line prints true. The transport policy sets redirect_http to true, which prints true on the first line directly. cors_mode() compares allowed_origin to "*"; because the origin is now the exact host "https://app.example.com", it returns "locked-down" and the third line prints that. The final line computes redirect_http && hsts_max_age_secs > 0; with the redirect on and a non-zero two-year max-age, both terms hold and it prints true, which also encodes the rule that HSTS and the redirect must reinforce each other rather than contradict.

The program uses only struct definitions, two impl blocks, and println!, so it compiles and runs with the standard library alone. Running it prints exactly the four expected lines.

reviewAnswers.question: What is the practical difference between server-authenticated TLS and mTLS?
reviewAnswers.answer: In server-authenticated TLS only the server presents a certificate, so the client verifies the server's identity but the server learns nothing cryptographic about who the client is; this is the right model for browser-facing and public APIs. In mTLS both ends present certificates and each verifies the other, so the server obtains a verified peer identity at the handshake. The practical payoff of mTLS is only realized if that verified identity is then turned into a policy input (an authorization decision) somewhere explicit; otherwise it is just extra ceremony. mTLS therefore fits internal service-to-service hops where you want to authenticate the caller, not just encrypt the bytes.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should proxy-header trust be tied to a known network boundary instead of accepted from arbitrary callers?
reviewAnswers.answer: A header such as X-Forwarded-Proto is just bytes, and any client can set it to whatever it likes, so believing it unconditionally lets an attacker claim a plaintext request arrived over HTTPS. The value is trustworthy only when it was written by a proxy you operate and arrived through the specific hops you control, which is why forwarded-proto trust must be scoped to a known network boundary and stripped from anything arriving directly. Tying trust to the boundary means the app believes the forwarded scheme exactly when, and only when, a real termination point produced it. Without that scoping, forwarded-header trust becomes a way to forge the very security property the boundary exists to enforce.

reviewAnswers.question: When is HSTS a safe default, and when is it premature?
reviewAnswers.answer: HSTS is a safe default once the site is reliably served over HTTPS on the host (and its subdomains, if includeSubDomains is set), because it instructs browsers to refuse plaintext and prevents downgrade on later visits. It is premature when any part of the host still legitimately needs plaintext, when HTTPS is not yet stable across every subdomain that would be covered, or when you would set a long max-age before you are confident, because a browser that has cached the policy will refuse to connect over HTTP and you cannot quickly undo that. The pragmatic path is to enable HTTPS and the redirect first, confirm stability, then turn on HSTS, and only later raise the max-age and consider preload. HSTS should reinforce an already-working redirect, never substitute for one.

reviewAnswers.question: Why are local CA and CI trust bundles safer than skip-verification flags for HTTPS testing?
reviewAnswers.answer: A local CA plus an explicit trust bundle makes the client perform the same chain assembly and hostname verification it would in production, so a passing test is real evidence that the secure path works. A skip-verification flag removes exactly the checks TLS exists to provide, so the test proves only that a port answers, not that certificates, chains, or hostnames are correct. Skip-verify also teaches the team a shortcut that tends to leak from test harnesses into clients, where it silently disables protection. The local-CA approach keeps test trust behavior close to production while never normalizing an insecure bypass.

reviewAnswers.question: What makes certificate rotation a deployment problem as much as a cryptography problem?
reviewAnswers.answer: The cryptography of issuing a new certificate is the easy part; the hard part is the lifecycle around it, because a certificate is a secret with an expiry date and renewing it on disk is a different event from loading it into the running process. Rotation therefore requires distributing the new trust root before issuing leaves from it, overlapping old and new material so a mixed rollout does not reject valid peers, and reloading the certificate and trust bundle without taking the service offline. Each of those is a deployment and orchestration concern, and the classic failure is renewing the file but never reloading it, which no cryptographic check catches. That is why rotation needs observability (expiry horizon, reload-failure count, rejection rate) and a reload strategy, not just a working key.

reviewAnswers.question: When would you reach for a Rust-native TLS stack over the platform's native stack, and why is that a topology decision before it is an API decision?
reviewAnswers.answer: This question only arises once you have already decided to terminate TLS inside the process; if a load balancer, reverse proxy, or sidecar owns the public connection, the library choice belongs to that component, not to your service. Given in-process termination, prefer a Rust-native stack (rustls) when you want the same trust material and behavior everywhere: it carries its own roots, so a container, a CI runner, and a developer laptop validate chains identically and a minimal image does not surprise you with an empty or stale system store. Prefer the platform's native stack when you specifically want to inherit the operating system's trust store and certificate lifecycle, for example to honor enterprise-managed roots, OS-level revocation, or a corporate proxy CA without shipping that policy yourself. The decision is topological first because the real question is which component owns trust distribution and packaging, and only after that is settled does the choice reduce to which client or server API you write against.
